vignette: The memory arrives in August, just as the late-summer heat thickens over the south pasture. Clara is twenty-six. She walks the irrigation lines near the old grain silos, boots sinking into damp clay. The truck doors slide open. She fights. She breaks down. The world narrows to breath and mud. When the engine fades, she remains in the dirt, counting the minutes until the sun dips below the tree line. She does not run. She waits for a sound that never comes. Ten years later, she marries David, a quiet man who speaks in the steady cadence of seasons and soil. They build a life around planting and harvest. For decades, Clara works the land with mechanical precision. She drives the combine at dawn, her hands steady on the wheel, her eyes tracking the rows. The past sleeps in her shoulders, a coiled wire she tightens with every turn of the plow. She drinks black coffee. She laughs at David's jokes. She walks the fence lines. But when a pickup truck backs up behind the house, her breath stops mid-cavity. She tells no one. Now, at sixty-nine, Clara sits across from me in a sunlit office. Her work gloves rest on her knee, the leather cracked, stained with soil she refuses to wash away. She speaks in a low, measured voice, describing the last three months. Since the early frost came early, the fields lie fallow, and the silence in the house feels heavier. She stops at the edge of the tree line during morning walks, her hands trembling as she scans the horizon for a vehicle that isn't there. She avoids the grain silos now, taking a three-mile detour through the county road, though she knows it adds forty minutes to her route. At night, she sleeps in the guest room. David rests a hand on her shoulder, and she flinches before she can stop herself. He stops reaching for her. She tells me this without tears, her gaze fixed on the dust motes in the window. "I'm still out there," she says. "Still kneeling in that dirt, waiting for the sun to move." She wakes at 3 a.m. with her heart hammering, the taste of copper in her mouth. She counts the fence posts along the eastern boundary until her breathing slows. She no longer enjoys the taste of strawberries. She flinches when the mail carrier's keys jingle at the porch. She tells me about the dream she's had every full moon for forty-three years: the silo door creaking open, and a hand reaching out to pull her inside. She wakes dry, but her body is drenched. She stops going to the hardware store. She tells David to drive past the county road during harvest. She sits in her truck with the engine running, hands white-knuckled on the wheel, watching a man in a flannel shirt load firewood into his bed, her throat closing until she drives away. She folds her gloves neatly on the arm of the chair. The sun has shifted. She thanks me for the tea, though she barely touches it. When she stands, her knees crack, and she pauses at the door, looking back at the empty chair across from her. "I used to know how to read the soil," she says softly. "Now I only know how to brace for impact."
